summary: This standards-track document revises RFC 1006 and describes how ISO Transport Services can run over TCP on IPv4 or IPv6. It also defines some new features not present in RFC 1006.

eli5.summary: A way for an older kind of delivery service to ride on the modern Internet trucks.

questions: how does itot differ from rfc 1006
subtitle: How to run the ISO Transport Service over TCP, so OSI applications can work on IPv4 and IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: Applications written for the ISO Transport Service needed a way to run over TCP/IP without each one being ported separately, and RFC 1006, the earlier answer, lacked features and needed refining.
tldr.mechanism: ITOT layers the ISO Transport Protocol (classes 0 and 2) on top of TCP, treating TCP as a connection-oriented network service and wrapping each transport message in a small TPKT header that marks where it starts and ends.
tldr.outcome: Class 0 keeps the installed base of RFC 1006 users working, while class 2 adds independent normal and expedited data channels and explicit disconnection. It updates RFC 1006 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 2126 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1006, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its abstract says it will eventually supersede RFC 1006.

sections.title: Why Layer ISO Transport over TCP
sections.content:
There are two ways to bring ISO applications to a TCP/IP or IPv6 network. One is to port every application separately and build local protocols on top of TCP. The other is to layer the ISO Transport Service over TCP/IP, which solves the problem for every application that uses that service. This RFC takes the second approach.

It rests on layer independence: if a layer keeps offering the same service, the layer above it is unaffected by what happens underneath. So the document presents a transport service that looks identical to the one in ISO 8072, but implements the ISO 8073 Transport Protocol on top of TCP (over IPv4 or IPv6) instead of the ISO Network Service.

The basis is RFC 1006. The goal is to change RFC 1006 and ISO 8073 as little as possible while improving performance, widening applicability and protecting the installed base. The document must be read together with the ISO standards, because it only specifies the differences. The well-known TCP port 102 is reserved for hosts that implement it, although the protocol does not require port 102 for every connection.
sections.eli5: Instead of rebuilding every game to work on a new console, you make one adapter that lets all the old games plug in. That is what this document describes.

sections.title: The Model: TCP as the Network Service
sections.content:
In the ISO model, the Transport Service Provider runs the ISO Transport Protocol over a Network Service, either connection-oriented (CONS) or connectionless (CLNS). In the ITOT model the ISO 8073 protocol, with some modifications, runs over TCP, and TCP stands in for the connection-oriented network service.

The mapping uses a few simple rules. To open a network connection, the transport provider does an active TCP open to the server's IPv4 or IPv6 address and port. A server does a passive open, and a successful connection counts as an implicit connect response. Sending data means putting a transport message into a TPKT and sending it over TCP. Releasing a connection simply closes the TCP connection, and a TCP error also produces a disconnect indication. Other service parameters are ignored.

Two variants are defined, Class 0 over TCP and Class 2 over TCP. The transport service itself is ISO 8072 with two changes: the Quality of Service parameter is not defined, and non-disruptive transport disconnection is available. Other ISO transport classes are not forbidden over TCP, but they are out of scope.
sections.eli5: TCP is the road, and the ISO transport is the delivery driver. The driver asks the road for a trip, hands over the packages, and ends the trip by closing the connection.

sections.title: The TPKT Packet Header
sections.content:
TCP delivers a continuous stream of octets with no boundaries, but ISO transport expects discrete units. ITOT therefore wraps each transport protocol data unit (TPDU) in a TPKT, which is a header followed by the TPDU. The header looks the same for every TPDU type.

  • version: 8 bits, value 3.
  • reserved: 8 bits, value 0.
  • packet length: 16 bits, the length of the entire TPKT in octets, header included.

The reserved field should be ignored on input, to avoid interoperability problems with RFC 1006. The version stays at 3 so existing RFC 1006 implementations that insist on version 3 can still talk to ITOT.
sections.eli5: TCP is a long ribbon with no breaks. The TPKT header is like a label on each message that says how long it is, so the receiver knows where one message ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Class 0 and Class 2 Procedures
sections.content:
Class 0 provides connection setup with negotiation, data transfer with segmentation and protocol error reporting. Its flow control and disconnection come from TCP, so disconnection is disruptive and there is no explicit transport disconnect. The ITOT changes add connect data in the CR and CC messages, optional expedited data, and a maximum TPDU size of 65531 octets, which is also the default. Expedited data in Class 0 uses a non-standard ED TPDU sent in-band on the same TCP connection, with 1 to 16 octets of user data.

Class 2 adds explicit transport disconnection and is meant for applications that need normal and expedited data kept independent. It can negotiate expedited data, expedited data acknowledgement (EA TPDUs), non-blocking expedited data, and a choice of two ways to set up a separate TCP connection for expedited data: Forward Connection (from ISO 8073) or Reverse Connection (new here). Explicit flow control must not be negotiated, and multiplexing is not supported.

With non-blocking expedited data, the sender sends each ED TPDU on both TCP connections and the receiver delivers the copy from the connection with the higher count. Disconnects come in two kinds, using DR and DC TPDUs: a disruptive disconnect with reason code normal (80 hex), and a non-disruptive one that also sets Additional Information to 80 hex and requires already-submitted TPDUs to be delivered first.
sections.eli5: Class 0 is a single-lane road where everything travels together. Class 2 can add a second fast lane for urgent messages, and lets either side politely say goodbye before hanging up.

sections.title: Negotiating Class and Options
sections.content:
ITOT requires implementations to support ISO 8073 option negotiation, including class negotiation. The initiator proposes a preferred class and may propose an alternative; the responder picks one. If the preferred class is not chosen, the initiator adjusts when the connect confirm arrives. A request for class 2 with class 0 as an alternative may be answered with either; class 2 with no alternative gets class 2.

Class 2 features are selected by bits of the Additional Option parameter: bit 1 for the transport expedited data service, bit 4 for Reverse (set) or Forward (clear) Connection, bit 6 for expedited data acknowledgement, and bit 7 for non-blocking expedited data. Every default is off, and the all-zero default gives an RFC 1006-like service with explicit disconnection.

The RFC adds practical advice. Because the default maximum TPDU size can break an ISO negotiation rule, the CC TPDU should always state the size. TCP keep-alive is strongly suggested so that a lost connection gets reported, and the Nagle algorithm should be disabled with the TCP_NODELAY socket option for performance.
sections.eli5: Before starting, the two sides agree on the rules, like picking which games and house rules to use. If they cannot agree on the fancy version, they fall back to the simple one.

sections.title: Addresses for ITOT
sections.content:
ITOT access point addresses can be written as printable strings or as OSI Network Addresses (NSAPs). A string address specifies an IP address (IPv4 or IPv6) and an optional TCP port number. RFC 1278 covers the string form for IPv4, and an update for IPv6 was still in progress when this RFC was written.

For NSAP encoding, RFC 1277 applies to IPv4. For IPv6, a separate document defines how to embed an IPv6 address in an OSI NSAP address. For ITOT addresses the default selector is the value '10000000'B. Since an IPv6 address can encode an IPv4 address, that format can carry IPv4 ITOT addresses too.
sections.eli5: Every mailbox needs an address. These rules say how to write the address of an ITOT service, using either the regular Internet address or the older OSI style.

sections.title: Interoperability with RFC 1006
sections.content:
The TPKT version stays at 3 because the changes do not conflict with RFC 1006, and changing it would stop RFC 1006 implementations that require version 3 from interoperating.

One consequence is class negotiation. Class 2 is new, so the need to negotiate between class 2 and class 0 is new too. Some RFC 1006 implementations cannot negotiate classes. A class 2 connect request with no alternative could therefore be answered with a class 0 connect confirm, and the initiator should then reject that confirm as ISO 8073 specifies.

Class 0 also no longer allows the credit and TPDU-NR fields to be ignored on input, which brings it in line with ISO 8073 encoding rules; RFC 1006 had inconsistent rules here.
sections.eli5: The new truck still uses the same plug as the old one, so old equipment keeps working. The only catch is that a few old machines do not understand the newest buttons.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not address security specifically. It says that operation of the protocol is no more and no less secure than operation of TCP and the ISO 8073 protocols, and points readers there for further reading. ITOT adds no authentication or encryption of its own.
sections.eli5: This adapter does not add a lock. It is exactly as safe as the truck and the driver already were.
